original_title: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub

existing.title: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub
existing.description_short: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub
existing.description_long: On January 31, 2025, President Trump sent a letter to Federal Election Commission Chair Ellen Weintraub — a Democratic commissioner who had been an outspoken critic of Trump's campaign finance violations — stating You are hereby removed as a Member of the Federal Election Commission, effective immediately. Weintraub publicly rejected the removal as illegal, noting that no president had ever fired an FEC commissioner and that the Federal Election Campaign Act contained no firing authority for the president. Republican former FEC Chair Trevor Potter called the action contrary to law, noting that Trump was free to nominate a replacement but could not simply fire a sitting commissioner. The timing was significant: the FEC was preparing to consider complaints against Trump's 2024 campaign and against Elon Musk's $277 million in political spending. Weintraub lost her email, computer, and cellphone access by February 7. The move was part of a broader pattern of firing independent agency members and preceded the eventual July 2026 Supreme Court ruling that gave presidents expanded power to fire independent agency members.

original_title: Alien Enemies Act Deportations: 137 Venezuelans Sent to CECOT Without Any Due Process

existing.title: Alien Enemies Act Deportations: 137 Venezuelans Sent to CECOT Without Any Due Process
existing.description_short: Alien Enemies Act Deportations: 137 Venezuelans Sent to CECOT Without Any Due Process
existing.description_long: On March 15–16, 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act — not used since World War II — to deport 137 Venezuelan nationals to El Salvador's CECOT prison with no notice, no hearings, and no opportunity to challenge removal. Federal Judge James Boasberg had issued a temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, and evidence emerged that planes carrying detainees had been ordered to continue to El Salvador even after the TRO was issued. In June 2025, Boasberg ruled in a sweeping opinion that the men had been plainly deprived of due process rights, comparing their situation to a Kafka novel: Perhaps the President lawfully invoked the Alien Enemies Act. Perhaps, moreover, Defendants are correct that Plaintiffs are gang members. But there is simply no way to know for sure, as the CECOT Plaintiffs never had any opportunity to challenge the Government's say-so. The Supreme Court unanimously agreed the men were entitled to notice and the opportunity to challenge removal before deportation. The administration had given some detainees as little as 24 hours notice.

existing.description_short: Trump Tower Russia Meeting: Don Jr. Takes a Meeting to Get Dirt on Clinton
existing.description_long: On June 9, 2016, Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, and then-campaign chairman Paul Manafort met at Trump Tower in New York with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya, after British music publicist Rob Goldstone emailed Trump Jr. that the meeting would provide official documents and information that would incriminate Hillary as part of Russia and its government's support for Mr. Trump. Trump Jr. responded by email: If it's what you say I love it especially later in the summer. The meeting was attended by at least eight people, including a former Soviet intelligence officer. Trump Jr. initially told the Senate Judiciary Committee he could not recall discussing it with his father. The meeting — kept secret until the New York Times reported it in July 2017, prompting Trump Jr. to release his emails — represented the most direct documented evidence of the Trump campaign's willingness to accept foreign interference in a U.S. election. The Senate Intelligence Committee later concluded in 2020 that Manafort's sharing of internal polling data with a Russian associate with GRU ties constituted a grave counterintelligence threat.

original_title: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists

existing.title: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists
existing.description_short: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists
existing.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order gutting the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), Voice of America's parent. By the morning of March 15, all 1,300 VOA employees had been placed on paid administrative leave, barred from the building and their equipment. DOGE operative Gavin Kliger — a former Twitter engineer — had been spotted inside VOA headquarters weeks earlier. VOA director Michael Abramowitz stated: For the first time in 83 years, the storied Voice of America is being silenced. Kari Lake, Trump's loyalist USAGM adviser, signed termination notices and canceled the agency's 15-year lease. VOA had operated continuously since 1942, originally to counter Nazi propaganda, and reached an estimated 247 million people weekly in 47 languages. Russian state media celebrated the shutdown; China's state press called VOA a dirty rag. The National Press Club said the action undermines America's long-standing commitment to a free press. Courts had blocked similar USAGM dismantlement attempts during Trump's first term. The shutdown left audiences across authoritarian states without access to independent, U.S.-funded journalism precisely when such coverage mattered most.

existing.description_long: On June 17, 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel published a post claiming the FBI had located alarming documents alleging Chinese Communist Party interference in the 2020 election. Patel said he had immediately declassified the material and shared it with Sen. Chuck Grassley. The documents centered on an unverified 2020 tip from an anonymous confidential informant claiming China mass-produced fake driver's licenses for a mail-in ballot scheme. NBC News and election law experts noted the tip was never substantiated: the only evidence Patel cited was CBP seizures of fake IDs from China, which CBP itself attributed to underage college students seeking to purchase alcohol. Election law expert Rick Hasen said Patel's post might feed the MAGA base but amounted to promoting an uncorroborated story of unknown origin with no evidence that anything actually happened. Two former senior FBI officials noted the bureau receives hundreds of tips daily, many unverified, and one warned that publicizing this information played into the hands of our foreign enemies. No evidence of widespread 2020 voter fraud has been found by any investigation, including those conducted by Trump-appointed officials.

existing.title: Clean Power Plan 2.0 Gutted — EPA Proposes Eliminating All GHG Standards for Power Plants
existing.description_short: Clean Power Plan 2.0 Gutted — EPA Proposes Eliminating All GHG Standards for Power Plants
existing.description_long: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, flanked by Republican lawmakers at EPA headquarters, proposed repealing all greenhouse gas emissions standards for the U.S. power sector under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act — effectively eliminating both the 2015 Obama-era standards for new fossil fuel plants and Biden's 2024 Clean Power Plan 2.0 emission guidelines for existing coal, oil, and gas plants. The proposal also moved to repeal 2024 amendments to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards that had been requiring coal plants to reduce brain-damaging mercury emissions. Zeldin claimed the rollbacks would save $120 million per year for electric utilities. Environmental groups countered that the repeals would increase cancer-causing and neurotoxic air pollution, lock in decades of carbon emissions, and kill thousands of Americans prematurely each year from worsened air quality. EPA had telegraphed the move on March 12, 2025, when Zeldin announced it as part of what he called the most consequential day of deregulation in U.S. history. A public hearing on the GHG repeal was held July 8, 2025, with EPA planning to finalize the rule by spring 2026.

existing.description_short: Riyadh Sellout: Trump Negotiates Ukraine's Fate with Russia, Excluding Europe and Kyiv

Russia used the talks to harden demands, insisting NATO cancel its 2008 promise to eventually admit Ukraine, and demanding territorial concessions. Trump had already ruled out NATO membership for Ukraine, demanded Ukraine surrender occupied territory, and proposed transferring vast portions of Ukrainian natural resources to the United States. European leaders warned that Trump appeared to believe giving Putin much of what he wants in Europe was the best path forward, effectively rewarding illegal aggression and demolishing 80 years of post-war security architecture.

existing.description_short: DOGE Copied All 548 Million SSNs to Unsecured Cloud Without Oversight
existing.description_long: In August 2025, Social Security Administration Chief Data Officer Charles Borges filed a whistleblower complaint with Congress alleging that DOGE officials employed as SSA staff had copied the entire NUMIDENT database — containing 548 million Social Security numbers along with names, addresses, dates of birth, parents' names, and other identifying information for every living and dead American who ever had an SSN — to a custom Amazon Web Services cloud environment that lacked any verified security oversight. The transfer occurred after the Supreme Court's June 6, 2025 ruling lifted a lower-court injunction blocking DOGE's SSA access. The acting chief information security officer had formally flagged the request as high risk and warned it could make Americans vulnerable to identity theft, but DOGE-affiliated CIO Aram Moghaddassi and Michael Russo approved the transfer anyway, arguing the business need is higher than the security risk. No independent security monitoring was in place; no one outside the DOGE group had insight into the code being executed against live SSA production data. Borges received no response to his security concerns from DOGE-affiliated staff. The SSA's spokesperson disputed the characterization but confirmed the environment existed.

existing.title: Trump Pressures Texas Redistricting to Flip 5 Democratic House Seats, Igniting National Map-Drawing Arms Race
existing.description_short: Trump Pressures Texas Redistricting to Flip 5 Democratic House Seats, Igniting National Map-Drawing Arms Race
existing.description_long: In July 2025, at Trump's direct urging, Texas Republicans undertook an extraordinary mid-decade redraw of the state's congressional districts, targeting five Democratic-held U.S. House seats with the explicit goal of protecting the GOP's fragile House majority ahead of the 2026 midterms — a move upending decades of precedent against mid-cycle partisan redistricting. Trump applied direct pressure to multiple other Republican-controlled legislatures; in Indiana, Lieutenant Governor Micah Beckwith confirmed that unnamed Trump administration officials threatened the state's federal funding if it refused to redistrict. existing.title: US Citizens Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez and Jose Hermosillo Detained by ICE Despite Documentation
existing.description_short: US Citizens Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez and Jose Hermosillo Detained by ICE Despite Documentation
existing.description_long: A documented pattern of ICE detaining American citizens swept through 2025. Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez, 20, born in Georgia, was arrested on April 16 during a traffic stop in Florida under a state law that a federal judge had already suspended on April 4. He presented his Social Security card and Georgia REAL ID to police but was held for more than 30 hours. ICE placed a detainer on the jail even after a judge found no probable cause. DHS falsely claimed Lopez-Gomez had identified himself as undocumented. Jose Hermosillo, 19, of Albuquerque, was arrested by Border Patrol in Tucson on April 9 while visiting with his girlfriend — 70 miles from the Mexican border — and held for 10 days before his family secured his release by providing proof of citizenship. DHS alleged Hermosillo told an agent he was born in Mexico; Hermosillo denied it, and attorneys noted he has a learning disability. In May 2026, a top ICE official stated at a border security conference: Since the start of this administration, we have not had any arrests of U.S. citizens... That's happened zero times — a claim directly contradicted by available evidence.

original_title: Steel and Aluminum Tariffs Doubled to 50%, Gutting Downstream Industries

existing.title: Steel and Aluminum Tariffs Doubled to 50%, Gutting Downstream Industries
existing.description_short: Steel and Aluminum Tariffs Doubled to 50%, Gutting Downstream Industries
existing.description_long: On June 4, 2025, Trump doubled U.S. tariffs on all steel and aluminum imports from 25% to 50% — among the highest metal duties in American history — just months after reinstating the original 25% rates in February. The stated goal was protecting domestic steel and aluminum producers, but economic analysis was clear about the consequences for downstream industries. A study found Trump's first-term steel tariffs created roughly 1,000 jobs in the steel sector while destroying 75,000 jobs in steel-using industries like manufacturing, construction, and auto parts. The 50% tariff added an estimated $2,000+ in production costs per vehicle. The aluminum tariff alone added $3,000 to the cost of an F-150 truck. John Deere cited $300 million in tariff-related costs in August 2025 and announced layoffs at Illinois and Iowa plants. Companies like Jordan Manufacturing in Belding, Michigan, saw steel prices rise 5%–10% and were forced to raise customer prices 8%–14%. The Tax Foundation's Erica York said: It's just very foolish to double down on this type of tariff in particular. Canada's steel and aluminum industry faced mass layoffs and investment deferrals. U.S. construction contracted 3.6% in long-run projections from the Yale Budget Lab.

existing.description_short: Green Card Holders Detained for Decades-Old Minor Crimes; LPRs Fear Leaving US
existing.description_long: Under Trump's second term, Customs and Border Protection and ICE sharply escalated enforcement against lawful permanent residents upon reentry, targeting people with decades-old criminal records that had previously been overlooked. Lewelyn Dixon, a 64-year-old Filipina legal permanent resident, was arrested at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and held for nearly three months after she disclosed a past workplace theft conviction from years prior, despite having lived blamelessly in her American community since. Her attorney noted he had handled three similar cases since February 2025 alone — unprecedented in his 12-year career. The pattern extended to Green Card holders with minor resolved records facing surprise detention when attempting to re-enter from international travel. Yunseo Chung, a 21-year-old Korean American Columbia University student who had lived in the U.S. since age seven as a lawful permanent resident, had her LPR status revocation initiated by DHS over pro-Palestinian protest participation. A federal judge ruled on March 25, 2025 that Chung could not be detained while fighting the revocation. Immigration attorneys reported a flood of clients asking whether they could safely leave the country at all — a chilling effect on the freedom of movement of 13 million legal permanent residents.

existing.description_short: Tariffs Weaponized for Corporate Allies: Chevron, Starlink in Trade Deals
existing.description_long: Internal documents obtained by The Washington Post in August 2025 revealed that Trump's trade team had weaponized tariff negotiations to secure business advantages for politically connected corporations. In eight-page supplemental negotiating objectives for trade talks with India, U.S. officials demanded India halt oil purchases from Russia — or face 50% tariffs — while separately pushing India, Taiwan, and Indonesia to purchase more American military equipment. Most remarkably, the documents showed Chevron's business interests were embedded directly in trade negotiating objectives with multiple foreign governments, asking them to avoid regulations that could harm Chevron's operations. Elon Musk's Starlink was flagged for favorable telecommunications licensing treatment abroad, including waiving physical-presence requirements in some markets. Israel and Australia were pressed to remove Chinese control from key ports. African and South American nations were pushed to limit Chinese telecom and military ties. Cambodia was told tariff relief was contingent on U.S. Navy port access. Officials described the scope as shocking. The blending of personal corporate interests, political alliances, and ostensibly public trade policy represented what critics called a textbook crony capitalist system in which tariff rates were effectively for sale to those who provided the right political or business concessions.

original_title: Trump Freezes $175M to UPenn Over Lia Thomas, Forces Record Erasure

existing.title: Trump Freezes $175M to UPenn Over Lia Thomas, Forces Record Erasure
existing.description_short: Trump Freezes $175M to UPenn Over Lia Thomas, Forces Record Erasure
existing.description_long: On March 19, 2025, the Trump administration announced it was suspending approximately $175 million in federal funding to the University of Pennsylvania — money drawn from the Department of Defense and the Department of Health and Human Services — over the school's past support of transgender swimmer Lia Thomas, who had last competed for Penn in 2022, three years earlier. Thomas had won the 2022 NCAA championship in the women's 500-yard freestyle, making her the first transgender woman to win an NCAA swimming championship. A White House official cited Thomas's access to the locker room as part of the justification. After months of standoff, on July 1, 2025, the Trump administration released the frozen funds after Penn reached an agreement with the federal government that included blocking transgender athletes from female sports teams going forward and — in a historically unprecedented act — erasing the NCAA championship records set by Thomas. The administration used financial coercion to compel a private university to retroactively revise the historical athletic record to conform to its ideological preferences. Penn students and faculty held protests against the capitulation. The episode set a chilling precedent for academic and institutional autonomy under federal funding pressure.

original_title: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased

existing.title: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased
existing.description_short: Trump Kills Methane Fee — Oil and Gas Industry's $900-Per-Ton Pollution Charge Erased
existing.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed H.J.Res. 35 — a Congressional Review Act joint resolution — into law as Public Law 119-2, nullifying EPA's Waste Emissions Charge rule that had imposed a $900-per-ton fee on oil and gas producers releasing excess methane, a fee that would have escalated to $1,500 per ton by 2026. The WEC had been a centerpiece of the Inflation Reduction Act's climate provisions, representing the first-ever federal price on methane pollution, which traps 80 times more heat per molecule than CO2 over a 20-year period. The House had passed the resolution February 26, 2025, and the Senate followed party-line 52-47 on February 27, with the repeal introduced by Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX). On May 12, 2025, EPA formally removed the WEC regulations from the Code of Federal Regulations. Scientists estimated the methane fee, had it remained in force, would have incentivized dramatic reductions in leaks from the roughly 900,000 U.S. oil and gas wells — methane being responsible for roughly 30% of current global warming. The repeal was celebrated by major oil and gas trade groups and came the same week the administration was proposing separate rollbacks on power plant emissions and vehicle standards.
